section_title.text: 3.1. Microstructure of the as-cast $C o _ { 1. 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1. 5 } T i _ { 0. 5 } M o _ { x }$ alloys

context_before.text: Fig. 1 illustrates the XRD patterns of the as-cast ${ \mathsf { C o } } _ { 1. 5 } { \mathsf { C r F e } }.$ $\mathsf { N i } _ { 1. 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0. 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { x } \left(x = 0, 0. 1, 0. 5, 0. 8 \right)$ alloys. In this study, all these alloys basically belong to a simple FCC solid-solution structure. However, as Mo content in $\mathrm { C o _ { 1. 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1. 5 } T i _ { 0. 5 } M o _ { \lambda } }$ alloys increases up to 0.5 and 0.8 mol, the small peaks slightly on the left and right of the matrix FCC in XRD patterns are identified as Cr and Mo rich sigma (r) phase. As the Mo content decreases in these alloys, the peak intensities also change due to the lattice distortion caused by the different atomic size and still remains in FCC structure [45]. There is also no tendency to form complex or multiple phases when increasing the number of constituent elements. Because the wavelength of X-ray is constant $\left(\lambda = 1. 5 4 \AA \right)$, from the angle (h) and plane (h k l) of each diffraction peak, a set of lattice parameter can be calculated by Bragg’s law. These values of lattice parameter were plotted against $\cos ^ { 2 } \theta,$, and the precise parameter of alloy (a) can be estimated by least squares and extrapolation method [52]. The lattice parameters of $\mathrm { C o _ { 1. 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1. 5 } T i _ { 0. 5 } M o } _ { x } \left(x = 0, 0. 1, 0. 5, 0. 8 \right)$ alloys in this study are about 3.59 Å. Fig. 2 shows the SEM images of the as-cast $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1. 5 } \mathrm { C r F e N i } _ { 1. 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0. 5 } \mathrm { M o } _ { x }$ alloys, which are composed of dendrites and interdentrites. According to the EDS analyses as listed in Table 2, the interdendrite (lighter phase) of the as-cast $\mathrm { C o } _ { 1. 5 } \mathrm { C r F } { \mathrm { - } }$ $\mathrm { e N i } _ { 1. 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0. 5 } \mathrm { M o } _ { x } \left(x = 0, 0. 1 \right)$ alloy is Ni and Ti rich phase, and dendrite (darker phase) is Fe and Cr rich phase. Table 3 lists chemical mixing enthalpy $(\Delta H ^ { \mathrm { c h e m } })$ of a pair of atoms [53–55]. As can be seen in Table 3, Ni and Ti have the larger negative enthalpy in the alloy. Thus, they are likely to aggregated in the interdendrite phase. When increasing the Mo content in the ${ \mathsf { C o } } _ { 1. 5 } { \mathrm { C r F e N i } } _ { 1. 5 } { \mathrm { T i } } _ { 0. 5 } { \mathrm { M o } } _ { x } \ (x = 0. 5$ 0.8) alloys, the interdendrites are rich in Cr and Mo, while the dendrites are rich in Co and Ni.
As listed in Table 3, Mo element has weaker binding force to other constituent elements than Fe, Co, Ni, Ti, and Cr. However, the chemical analysis of that ‘‘interdendrites” is presented in

The tendency to r phase formation of an austenitic stainless steel can be known from the equivalent chromium content (ECC) equation [56]:

If the ECC is greater than 17–18%, the steel is susceptible to r phase formation. In this case, according to the ECC equation mentioned above, the ECC values for the $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1. 5 } \mathrm { C r F e N i } _ { 0. 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0. 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { 0. 5 }$ and $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1. 5 } \mathrm { C r F e N i } _ { 1. 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0. 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { 0. 8 }$ alloys were 43.73% and 53.63%, respectively. This indicates that an ECC of above 43% is susceptible to form that phase. Moreover, according to Conejero et al. [57], the Cr and Mo rich r phase forms mainly at grain boundaries in 316L type stainless steels and full austenitic alloys during the solidification.

context_after.text: The obtained polarisation results (Table 4) have revealed that Mo addition tends to increase the corrosion current density of Mo-containing alloys in 0.5 M $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 }.$ These results are in disagreement with Hashimoto [69] who reported that in the active region of stainless steels, where preferential dissolution of iron and chromium occurred, the formation of the passive molybdenum oxide film was responsible for a large decrease of the current density. The opposite results were found by Bojinov et al. [70] in studies of the electrochemical behaviour of anodic films on pure Cr,

Fe–Cr alloys and Fe–Cr–Mo alloys in 1 M $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } S 0 _ { 4 }$ solution. The corrosion current density in the $\mathrm { C o _ { 1. 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1. 5 } T i _ { 0. 5 } M o _ { 0. 1 } }$ alloy is lower than that in the $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { C r F e N i } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { T i } _ { 0. 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { 0 }$ alloy, which may be attributed to the simultaneous presence of lower Cr and slightly higher Mo content (1.8 atom%) in the $\mathrm { C o _ { 1. 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1. 5 } T i _ { 0. 5 } M o _ { 0. 1 } }$ alloy (Table 2). As the Mo content increases from 0.5 to 0.8 mol in the high-entropy alloys, the interdendrite phase of the ${ \mathrm { C o } } _ { 1. 5 } { \mathrm { C r F e - } }$ $\mathsf { N i } _ { 1. 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0. 5 } \mathrm { M o } _ { x }$ alloys is a Cr and Mo rich r phase, and the dendrite is a Cr and Mo depleted phase. The r phase is probably the most studied and undesirable phase in a stainless steel. Formation of r phase can occur in the austenitic, ferritic, and duplex stainless steels. Especially in duplex stainless steels, the formation of r phase is accelerated by increased amount of Cr and Mo [71,72]. The formation of that phase not only causes losses in ductility and toughness of the steel, but also reduces its corrosion resistance by removing Cr and Mo from the austenitic matrix [73]. Conejero et al. [57] studied premature corrosion failure of a 316L stainless steel plate exposed to a $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } S 0 _ { 4 }$ environment. It was reported that a 316L stainless steel plate has failed due to the presence of r phase, which is deleterious to corrosion performance of the stainless steels in $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } S 0 _ { 4 }$ solution. Therefore, the $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { C r F e N i } _ { 1. 5 } \mathsf { T i } _ { 0. 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { x }$ $\left(x = 0. 5, 0. 8 \right)$ alloys possessed the lower corrosion current density in comparison with the Mo-free alloy in this study, which could be also attributed to the presence of r phase.

The product of the transpassive region of Mo depends on the pH of test solutions. Therefore, $\mathsf { M o O } _ { 4 } ^ { 2 \cdot }$ <sup></sup> is formed in NaOH solutions in this study.

The $\mathrm { C 0 _ { 1. 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1. 5 } T i _ { 0. 5 } M o } _ { x } \left(x = 0, 0. 1, 0. 5, \mathrm { a n d } 0. 8 \right)$ alloys achieve their corrosion resistance by formation of an oxide passive layer. It has been reported that Ni, Ti, Co, and their alloys resist corrosion by NaOH solutions [74]. For Ni and its alloys, the generally accepted Ni (II) oxide passive film contributes to retard the corrosion phenomenon by diminishing the corrosion current density $(i _ { \mathrm { c o r r } })$ although it is not the essential element to improve the passive properties of the alloys. The Ti and its alloys have good protective properties due to its compact, passive film that contains the protective titanium dioxide $(\mathrm { T i O } _ { 2 }),$ corrosion and passivation behaviour of Co and its alloys in aqueous NaOH solutions are covered by a stable passive film which consists ofCo (II) oxide/hydroxide. It has been reported that the content of Cr and Mo plays an important role in the corrosion resistance of stainless steels and nickel alloys [79–81]. For Fe–Ni–Cr–Mo stainless steel, such as 316 stainless steels, the relative effectiveness of Cr and Mo contents on pitting or crevice corrosion usually can be assessed qualitatively by pitting resistance equivalent (PRE), which is represented by the empirical equation [82]:

In this study, according to the PRE equation mentioned above, the PRE values for the pitting-resistant $\mathrm { C o _ { 1. 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1. 5 } T i _ { 0. 5 } M o _ { 0. 1 } }$ $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1. 5 } \mathrm { C r F e N i } _ { 1. 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0. 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { 0. 5 },$, and $\mathsf { C o } _ { 1. 5 } \mathrm { C r F e N i } _ { 1. 5 } \mathrm { T i } _ { 0. 5 } \mathsf { M o } _ { 0. 8 }$ alloys are 26.32, 59.05, and 79.31, respectively. The $\mathrm { C o _ { 1. 5 } C r F e N i _ { 1. 5 } T i _ { 0. 5 } M o _ { 0 } },$ alloy, which is susceptible to pitting corrosion, has PRE value 16.87. This indicates that a PRE of above 26 is crucial to protect the as-cast Mo-containing alloys from pitting corrosion in 1 M NaCl solution.
